chapters.title: Book Thirteen (1812) — Chapter XV
paragraphs: In the early days of October, another envoy came to Kutuzov with a letter from Napoleon proposing peace, falsely dated from Moscow, though Napoleon was already not far from Kutuzov on the old Kaluga road. Kutuzov replied as he had to Lauriston's earlier letter, saying there could be no question of peace.

Soon after, a report came in from Dorokhov's guerrilla detachment, operating to the left of Tarutino, that troops from Broussier's division had been spotted at Forminsk and, being separated from the main French army, could easily be destroyed. The soldiers and officers again demanded action. Generals on the staff, emboldened by the easy victory at Tarutino, urged Kutuzov to follow Dorokhov's suggestion. Kutuzov didn't think any offensive was necessary. The result was an inevitable compromise: a small detachment was sent to Forminsk to attack Broussier.

By a strange coincidence, this task—which turned out to be one of the most difficult and important of the campaign—was given to Dokhturov, that same modest little Dokhturov whom no one has ever described drawing up battle plans, charging in front of regiments, or showering decorations on batteries, and who was considered and spoken of as indecisive and lacking insight. Yet we find him in command at the most critical position in every engagement of the Russo-French wars from Austerlitz to 1813. At Austerlitz he was the last to hold the Augezd dam, rallying regiments and saving what he could when everyone was fleeing and not a single general remained in the rear guard. Ill with fever, he went to Smolensk with twenty thousand men to defend it against Napoleon's entire army. At the Malakhov Gate in Smolensk, he had barely dozed off in a bout of fever before being woken by the bombardment—and Smolensk held out all day. At Borodino, when Bagration was killed and nine-tenths of the men on the left flank had fallen and the full force of French artillery was directed there, the man sent to that spot was this same 'irresolute and unperceptive' Dokhturov—Kutuzov rushing to correct a mistake he'd made by first sending someone else. And the quiet little Dokhturov rode there, and Borodino became the greatest glory of the Russian army. Many heroes of that time have been celebrated in verse and prose, but about Dokhturov, scarcely a word has been said.

It was Dokhturov again who was sent to Forminsk and from there to Malo-Yaroslavets—the site of the last battle with the French, where the obvious disintegration of the French army began. We hear about many geniuses and heroes of that campaign, but about Dokhturov, nothing or almost nothing, and even that is said doubtfully. This silence about Dokhturov is the clearest proof of his merit.

It's natural for someone who doesn't understand how a machine works to assume that a wood shaving that has accidentally fallen into it and is bouncing around, interfering with its operation, must be its most important part. Someone who doesn't understand the machine's construction can't grasp that the small connecting cog, turning quietly, is one of the most essential parts—not the shaving that merely damages and hinders it.

On October tenth, Dokhturov had gotten halfway to Forminsk and stopped at the village of Aristovo, faithfully preparing to carry out his orders. Then the entire French army—having lurched convulsively toward Murat's position as if to give battle—suddenly and for no apparent reason veered left onto the new Kaluga road and began pouring into Forminsk, where previously only Broussier had been. At that point, Dokhturov had under his command, besides Dorokhov's detachment, the two small guerrilla bands of Figner and Seslavin.

On the evening of October eleventh, Seslavin arrived at Aristovo headquarters with a captured French guardsman. The prisoner said the troops entering Forminsk that day were the vanguard of the entire army—Napoleon was there, and the whole army had left Moscow four days earlier. That same evening, a house servant from Borovsk said he'd seen an enormous army entering the town. Cossacks from Dokhturov's detachment reported sighting the French Guards marching toward Borovsk. From all these reports, it was clear that where they had expected to find a single division, they now faced the entire French army, marching from Moscow in an unexpected direction along the Kaluga road. Dokhturov was unwilling to act, as it was no longer clear what he should do. He'd been ordered to attack Forminsk, but at that time only Broussier had been there—now the whole French army was there. Ermolov wanted to act on his own judgment, but Dokhturov insisted on getting instructions from Kutuzov. So it was decided to send a dispatch to the staff.

For this mission, they chose a capable officer named Bolkhovitinov, who was to explain the situation verbally as well as deliver a written report. Toward midnight, Bolkhovitinov received the dispatch and verbal instructions and galloped off to General Staff headquarters, accompanied by a Cossack with spare horses.

chapters.title: Book Thirteen (1812) — Chapter XVI
paragraphs: It was a warm, dark autumn night. It had been raining for four days. Having changed horses twice and galloped twenty miles in an hour and a half over a sticky, muddy road, Bolkhovitinov reached Litashevka after one in the morning. Dismounting at a cottage on whose wattle fence hung a sign reading GENERAL STAFF, he threw down his reins and entered a dark corridor.
'The general on duty—quickly! It's very important!' he said to someone who had risen and was sniffing in the dark passage.
'He's been very unwell since this evening, and this is the third night he hasn't slept,' the orderly whispered pleadingly. 'You should wake the captain first.'
'But this is very important—from General Dokhturov,' said Bolkhovitinov, finding the open door by feeling in the dark.
The orderly went in ahead and began waking someone.
'Your honor! Your honor! A courier!'
'What? What's that? From whom?' came a sleepy voice.
'From Dokhturov and Alexei Petrovich. Napoleon is at Forminsk,' said Bolkhovitinov, unable to see who was speaking in the dark but guessing from the voice that it wasn't Konovnitsyn.
The man who had been woken yawned and stretched.
'I don't like waking him,' he said, fumbling for something. 'He's very ill. Maybe this is just a rumor.'
'Here's the dispatch,' said Bolkhovitinov. 'My orders are to deliver it immediately to the general on duty.'

'Wait a moment, I'll light a candle. Where do you always hide the damn thing, you rascal?' said the voice of the stretching man to the orderly. (This was Shcherbinin, Konovnitsyn's adjutant.) 'I've found it, I've found it!' he added.
The orderly was striking a light, and Shcherbinin was fumbling for the candlestick.
'Oh, the disgusting creatures!' he said with revulsion.
By the light of the sparks, Bolkhovitinov saw Shcherbinin's youthful face as he held the candle, and the face of another man still asleep. This was Konovnitsyn.

When the flame of the sulfur splinter, kindled by the tinderbox, flared first blue then red, Shcherbinin lit the tallow candle—from which cockroaches that had been gnawing on it scurried away—and looked at the messenger. Bolkhovitinov was splattered all over with mud and had smeared his face by wiping it with his sleeve.
'Who sent the report?' asked Shcherbinin, taking the envelope.
'The intelligence is reliable,' said Bolkhovitinov. 'Prisoners, Cossacks, and scouts all confirm the same thing.'

'There's nothing for it—we'll have to wake him,' said Shcherbinin, rising and walking over to the man in the nightcap who lay covered by a greatcoat. 'Pyotr Petrovich!' he said. (Konovnitsyn didn't stir.) 'To the General Staff!' he said with a smile, knowing those words were sure to rouse him.

And indeed, the head in the nightcap lifted at once. On Konovnitsyn's handsome, resolute face, with cheeks flushed from fever, there lingered for a moment a faraway, dreamy expression—then he suddenly snapped to attention, and his face took on its usual calm, firm look.
'Well, what is it? From whom?' he asked immediately, without hurry, blinking at the light.

While listening to the officer's report, Konovnitsyn broke the seal and read the dispatch. He had barely finished before he lowered his legs in their woolen stockings to the dirt floor and began pulling on his boots. Then he took off his nightcap, combed his hair over his temples, and put on his cap.
'Did you get here quickly? Let's go to His Highness.'

Konovnitsyn had understood at once that this news was of great importance and that there was no time to lose. He didn't pause to consider whether it was good news or bad. That didn't interest him. He viewed the entire business of the war not through intelligence or reason but through something deeper. Within him lay a deep, unspoken conviction that all would be well—but that one must not rely on this, much less talk about it. One must simply attend to one's own work. And he did his work, giving it his full strength.

Pyotr Petrovich Konovnitsyn, like Dokhturov, seems to have been included merely for form's sake in the list of the so-called heroes of 1812—the Barclays, Raevskys, Ermolovs, Platovs, and Miloradoviches. Like Dokhturov, he had the reputation of being a man of very limited abilities, and like Dokhturov, he never drew up battle plans but was always found where things were most difficult. Since his appointment as general on duty, he always slept with his door open, with orders that every messenger be allowed to wake him. In battle he was always under fire, so that Kutuzov reproached him for it and was afraid to send him to the front. And like Dokhturov, he was one of those unnoticed cogs that, without noise or fuss, form the most essential parts of the machine.

Emerging from the hut into the damp, dark night, Konovnitsyn frowned—partly from a worsening pain in his head and partly at the unpleasant thought of how all those influential men on the staff would be stirred up by this news, especially Bennigsen, who had been at war with Kutuzov ever since Tarutino. He could already picture their suggestions, their quarrels, their orders and counter-orders. This prospect was disagreeable, though he knew it couldn't be avoided.

And indeed, Toll—the first person he went to with the news—immediately began laying out his plans to a general sharing his quarters, until Konovnitsyn, who had been listening in weary silence, reminded him that they needed to go see His Highness.

chapters.title: Book Thirteen (1812) — Chapter XVII
paragraphs: Kutuzov, like all old people, slept very little at night. He often dropped off unexpectedly during the day, but at night, lying on his bed fully clothed, he generally stayed awake thinking.
So he lay now on his bed, resting his large, heavy, scarred head on his plump hand, with his one good eye open, pondering and peering into the darkness.

Since Bennigsen—who corresponded with the Emperor and held more influence than anyone else on the staff—had begun avoiding him, Kutuzov felt more at ease about the possibility of himself and his troops being forced into useless offensive operations. The lesson of the Battle of Tarutino and the day before it, which Kutuzov remembered with pain, must, he thought, have some effect on others too.

'They must understand that we can only lose by attacking. Patience and time are my warriors, my champions,' thought Kutuzov. He knew that you shouldn't pick an apple while it's still green. It will fall by itself when ripe. But if you pick it unripe, you ruin the apple, damage the tree, and set your teeth on edge. Like an experienced hunter, he knew the beast was wounded—wounded as only the combined strength of Russia could have wounded it. But whether the wound was mortal remained an open question. Now, from the fact that Lauriston and Barthélemi had been sent, and from the guerrillas' reports, Kutuzov was almost sure the wound was fatal. But he needed more proof, and he had to wait.

'They want to run over and see how badly they've hurt it. Wait, and we'll see! All these maneuvers, all these advances!' he thought. 'What for? Only to make themselves look good. As if fighting were some kind of game. They're like children who can't give you a sensible account of what happened because they all want to show how well they can fight. But that's not what's needed now.'

'And what elaborate maneuvers they all propose to me! They seem to think that when they've considered two or three possibilities'—he recalled the general plan sent from Petersburg—'they've thought of everything. But the possibilities are endless.'

The unresolved question of whether the wound inflicted at Borodino was mortal had hung over Kutuzov's head for an entire month. On the one hand, the French had occupied Moscow. On the other, Kutuzov felt certain with his whole being that the terrible blow into which he and all of Russia had poured their strength must have been fatal. But he needed proof. He had waited a whole month and was growing more impatient every day. Lying on his bed during those sleepless nights, he did exactly what he criticized the younger generals for doing: he imagined every possible scenario. But unlike them, he saw thousands of possibilities instead of two or three, and based nothing on any of them. He imagined every conceivable movement of Napoleon's army—as a whole or in parts—against Petersburg, or against him, or to outflank him. He also considered the possibility he feared most: that Napoleon might turn his own weapon against him and simply stay in Moscow, waiting him out. Kutuzov even imagined the French army turning back through Medyn and Yukhnov. But the one thing he could not foresee was what actually happened: the insane, convulsive stampede of Napoleon's army during its first eleven days after leaving Moscow—a stampede that made possible what Kutuzov hadn't yet dared to imagine: the complete destruction of the French. Dorokhov's report about Broussier's division, the guerrillas' reports of distress in Napoleon's army, and rumors of preparations to leave Moscow all supported the idea that the French army was beaten and preparing to flee. But these were only suppositions, which seemed important to the younger men but not to Kutuzov. With his sixty years of experience, he knew the value of rumors, knew how readily people who want something will arrange all the news to confirm their wishes, and ignore everything that contradicts them. The more he wanted to believe, the less he allowed himself to. This question consumed all his mental energy. Everything else was mere routine—his conversations with the staff, his letters to Madame de Staël, his reading of novels, the distribution of awards, his correspondence with Petersburg, and so on. But the destruction of the French, which he alone foresaw, was his heart's one desire.
On the night of the eleventh of October, he lay propped on his arm, thinking about it.
There was movement in the next room, and he heard the footsteps of Toll, Konovnitsyn, and Bolkhovitinov.
'Hello—who's there? Come in, come in! What news?' the field marshal called out.
While a servant lit a candle, Toll communicated the substance of the news.
'Who brought it?' asked Kutuzov, and when the candle was lit, Toll was struck by the cold severity of his expression.
'There can be no doubt about it, Your Highness.'
'Call him in. Bring him here.'

Kutuzov sat up with one leg hanging off the bed and his large belly resting against the other leg, which was doubled under him. He squinted his seeing eye to scrutinize the messenger more carefully, as if trying to read in his face what occupied his own mind.

'Tell me, tell me, my friend,' he said to Bolkhovitinov in his low, aged voice, pulling together the shirt that gaped open on his chest. 'Come closer—closer. What news have you brought? Napoleon has left Moscow? Are you sure?'
Bolkhovitinov gave a detailed account of everything he had been told to report.
'Speak faster, faster! Don't torture me!' Kutuzov interrupted.

Bolkhovitinov told him everything and fell silent, awaiting orders. Toll started to say something, but Kutuzov stopped him. He tried to speak himself, but his face suddenly crumpled and wrinkled. He waved his arm at Toll and turned to the opposite side of the room, toward the corner darkened by the icons hanging there.
'O Lord, my Creator, You have heard our prayer...' he said in a trembling voice, with folded hands. 'Russia is saved. I thank You, O Lord!' And he wept.

chapters.title: Book Thirteen (1812) — Chapter XVIII
paragraphs: From the moment he received this news until the end of the campaign, all of Kutuzov's energy was directed toward restraining his troops—by authority, by cunning, and by pleading—from useless attacks, maneuvers, and clashes with the dying enemy. Dokhturov went to Malo-Yaroslavets, but Kutuzov lingered with the main army and gave orders for the evacuation of Kaluga—a retreat beyond that town seemed entirely possible to him.
Everywhere Kutuzov retreated, but the enemy, without waiting for his retreat, fled in the opposite direction.

Napoleon's historians describe his skillful maneuvers at Tarutino and Malo-Yaroslavets and speculate about what might have happened if Napoleon had managed to reach the rich southern provinces in time.

But setting aside the fact that nothing prevented him from advancing south (the Russian army wasn't blocking his way), the historians forget that nothing could have saved his army, because it already carried within itself the seeds of inevitable destruction. How could that army—which had found abundant supplies in Moscow and trampled them underfoot instead of preserving them, and which on arriving at Smolensk had looted provisions instead of storing them—how could such an army recover in Kaluga province, inhabited by the same kind of Russians who lived in Moscow, where fire had the same ability to consume whatever was set ablaze?
That army could not recover anywhere. Since the Battle of Borodino and the pillaging of Moscow, it had carried within itself the chemical elements of its own dissolution.

The members of what had once been an army—Napoleon himself and all his soldiers—fled without knowing where, each concerned only with escaping as quickly as possible from a situation whose hopelessness they all more or less vaguely sensed.

So at the council at Malo-Yaroslavets, when the generals pretended to deliberate and offered various opinions, all mouths were shut by the opinion of the plain-spoken soldier Mouton, who spoke last and said what they all felt: the only thing to do was get away as fast as possible. And no one—not even Napoleon—could argue against that truth they all recognized.

But though everyone realized they had to retreat, there remained a feeling of shame at admitting they had to flee. An outside jolt was needed to overcome that shame, and it came right on time. The French called it 'the Emperor's hurrah.'

The day after the council at Malo-Yaroslavets, Napoleon rode out early among the lines of his army with his marshals and escort, ostensibly to inspect the troops and the scene of the recent and upcoming battle. Some Cossacks out looking for plunder ran into the Emperor and very nearly captured him. What saved Napoleon wasn't the strength of his forces but the very thing that was destroying the French army: the lure of loot. The Cossacks went after the plunder, just as they had at Tarutino, leaving the men behind. Ignoring Napoleon, they chased the booty, and Napoleon managed to escape.

When 'the children of the Don' could so easily have captured the Emperor himself in the midst of his army, it was clear there was nothing to do but flee as fast as possible along the nearest, most familiar road. Napoleon, with his forty-year-old stomach, understood the hint. No longer feeling his former agility and boldness, and shaken by the fright the Cossacks had given him, he immediately agreed with Mouton and issued orders—as the historians tell us—to retreat along the Smolensk road.

That Napoleon agreed with Mouton, and that the army retreated, doesn't prove that Napoleon caused it to retreat. Rather, the forces influencing the entire army and directing it along the Mozhaysk (that is, the Smolensk) road were simultaneously acting on him as well.

chapters.title: Book Fourteen (1812) — Chapter XIX
paragraphs: A person in motion always invents a purpose for that motion. To be able to march a thousand miles, you must believe that something good awaits you at the end of those thousand miles. You need the prospect of a promised land to have the strength to keep moving.

For the French during their advance, the promised land had been Moscow. During their retreat, it was their homeland. But their homeland was too far away, and for someone traveling a thousand miles, it's absolutely necessary to set aside the final goal and tell yourself: 'Today I'll reach a place twenty-five miles ahead, where I'll rest for the night.' And during that first day's march, the resting place eclipses the ultimate destination and draws all your hopes and desires. The impulses felt by a single person are always magnified in a crowd.

For the French retreating along the old Smolensk road, the final goal—their homeland—was too remote. Their immediate goal was Smolensk, toward which all their desires and hopes, enormously intensified in the mass, propelled them onward. It wasn't that they knew plenty of food and fresh troops awaited them in Smolensk, nor were they told so (on the contrary, their officers and Napoleon himself knew that provisions there were scarce). But this was the only thing that could give them the strength to keep moving and endure their present suffering. So those who knew and those who didn't both deceived themselves and pushed on toward Smolensk as toward a promised land.

Reaching the highway, the French fled with astonishing energy and unheard-of speed toward their chosen goal. Besides the shared impulse that bound the entire French mass into one body and gave it a kind of energy, there was another force holding them together: their sheer numbers. As with the physical law of gravity, their enormous mass drew individual human atoms to itself. In their hundreds of thousands, they moved like an entire nation.

Each man wanted nothing more than to give himself up as a prisoner and escape the horror and misery. But on one hand, the gravitational pull of Smolensk drew every one of them in the same direction; on the other, an army corps can't surrender to a company. Though the French seized every opportunity to break away and surrender on the slightest decent pretext, such opportunities didn't always arise. Their very numbers and the speed of their movement made it not just difficult but impossible for the Russians to halt them. No mechanical force could hasten the process of decomposition beyond a certain point.
A lump of snow can't be melted all at once. There is a minimum time required, and no amount of heat can melt it faster. In fact, the more heat you apply, the harder the remaining snow becomes.

Of the Russian commanders, Kutuzov alone understood this. When the French army's flight along the Smolensk road became well established, what Konovnitsyn had foreseen on the night of the eleventh began to happen. Every senior officer wanted to distinguish himself—to cut off, seize, capture, and crush the French—and all clamored for action.
Kutuzov alone used all his power (and a commander in chief's power is very limited) to prevent an attack.

He couldn't tell them what we can say now: 'Why fight? Why block the road, losing our own men and inhumanely slaughtering miserable wretches? What's the point, when a third of their army has already melted away on the march from Moscow to Vyazma without a single battle?' But drawing on his years of wisdom, he told them what they could understand—about the golden bridge—and they laughed at him and slandered him, flinging themselves on, tearing at, and gloating over the dying beast.

Ermolov, Miloradovich, Platov, and others near the French at Vyazma couldn't resist their desire to cut off and smash two French corps. To inform Kutuzov of their intentions, they sent him a blank sheet of paper in an envelope.

And try as Kutuzov might to hold the troops back, the Russians attacked, trying to block the road. Infantry regiments, we are told, advanced with music playing and drums beating, and killed and lost thousands of men.
But they didn't cut off or capture anyone. The French army, closing ranks more tightly in the face of danger, continued to melt steadily away as it pursued its fatal path toward Smolensk.
